I met the curious stranger I am about to describe at Warwick Castle. Three things drew me to him: his straightforward simplicity, his astonishing knowledge of ancient armour, and the restful nature of his company, since he did all the talking. As quiet people often do, we found ourselves together at the back of the group being shown around, and he immediately began saying things that caught my interest. Speaking softly, pleasantly, and fluently, he seemed to slip almost imperceptibly out of this world and this time into a distant age and a long-forgotten country. Little by little, he cast such a spell over me that I seemed to walk among the ghosts, shadows, dust, and mildew of a dim antiquity, conversing with one of its surviving relics. He spoke of Sir Bedivere, Sir Bors de Ganis, Sir Launcelot of the Lake, Sir Galahad, and all the other great figures of the Round Table exactly as I would speak of my closest friends or enemies, or neighbours I knew well. And as he continued, how old he began to look—unspeakably old, faded, dry, musty, ancient! Presently he turned toward me and remarked, as casually as if discussing the weather or any other everyday subject:

‘You know about souls migrating from one body to another. Do you know about the transposition of eras—and bodies?’

I said I had never heard of it. He showed so little interest, just as people do when discussing the weather, that he did not even notice whether I answered. A brief silence followed, broken almost immediately by the monotonous voice of the paid guide:

‘Ancient coat of mail, dated to the sixth century, the time of King Arthur and the Round Table. Said to have belonged to Sir Sagramor le Desirous. Notice the round hole through the chain mail over the left breast. Unexplained. Thought to have been made by a bullet after firearms were invented—perhaps by Cromwell’s soldiers out of malice.’

My companion smiled. It was no modern smile, but one that must have fallen out of common use many centuries earlier. Apparently speaking to himself, he murmured:

‘Believe me, I saw it happen.’ After a pause he added, ‘I did it myself.’

By the time I recovered from the shock of those words, he had disappeared.

All that evening I sat beside my fire at the Warwick Arms, absorbed in dreams of the distant past, while rain battered the windows and wind roared around the eaves and corners. Now and then I opened old Sir Thomas Malory’s enchanting book, feasted on its rich supply of wonders and adventures, savoured the fragrance of its forgotten names, and returned to my dreams.

He said nothing about it, however, until their visitor had left for the night. As soon as he was gone, he turned to his daughter.

‘Jane, congratulations. You will be a very happy woman.’

Jane went straight to him, kissed him, and thanked him for his kindness.

‘You are a good girl,’ he answered, ‘and it gives me great pleasure to think of you so happily married. I have no doubt that you will get along wonderfully. Your characters are very much alike. You are both so willing to please that you will never decide anything; so easygoing that every servant will cheat you; and so generous that you will always spend more than you earn.’

‘I hope that won’t happen. For me to be careless or thoughtless with money would be unforgivable.’

‘Spend more than they earn! My dear Mr. Bennet,’ cried his wife, ‘what are you saying? He has four or five thousand a year, and probably more.’ Turning to her daughter, she added, ‘Oh, my dear, dear Jane, I’m so happy! I’m sure I won’t sleep a wink all night. I knew this would happen. I always said it must, in the end. I was certain you couldn’t be so beautiful for nothing! I remember thinking how likely you were to marry the moment I first saw him, when he came to Hertfordshire last year. Oh, he is the most handsome young man anyone ever saw!’

Wickham and Lydia were completely forgotten. Jane was now her favourite child by far. At that moment she cared about no one else. Jane’s younger sisters soon began asking her for pleasures she might be able to provide for them in the future.

Mary asked to use the library at Netherfield, while Kitty pleaded for a few balls there every winter.

From then on, Bingley naturally visited Longbourn every day. He often arrived before breakfast and always stayed until after supper, unless some dreadful neighbour, impossible to dislike enough, had invited him to dinner and he felt obliged to accept.

Elizabeth now had little chance to talk with her sister. Whenever Bingley was there, Jane had no attention left for anyone else. But Elizabeth found herself very useful to both of them during the hours when they were sometimes forced to be apart. Whenever Jane was absent, Bingley stayed close to Elizabeth for the pleasure of talking about her. And whenever Bingley had left, Jane always sought the same comfort.

‘He has made me so happy,’ she told Elizabeth one evening, ‘by telling me he had absolutely no idea I was in London last spring!’

And if he asked why I wanted it, or why I believed I had any right to it, I would tell him, however little he cared for such poor dreams, that I had loved Estella deeply and for a long time. Although I had lost her and must spend my life grieving, anything that concerned her was still closer and dearer to me than anything else in the world. When I saw that Mr. Jaggers remained motionless and silent, apparently unmoved by this appeal, I turned to Wemmick. ‘Wemmick, I know you have a kind heart. I have seen your pleasant home, your elderly father, and all the innocent, cheerful amusements that restore you after your working life. Please speak to Mr. Jaggers on my behalf, and explain that, considering all the circumstances, he ought to be more open with me!’

I have never seen two men exchange stranger looks than Mr. Jaggers and Wemmick did after this appeal. For a moment I feared that Wemmick would lose his job on the spot. But that fear faded when I saw something like a smile loosen Mr. Jaggers’s expression, and Wemmick grow more confident.

‘What’s all this?’ Mr. Jaggers asked. ‘You have an elderly father, and you have pleasant, playful habits?’

‘Well,’ Wemmick replied, ‘as long as I don’t bring them here, what difference does it make?’

‘Pip,’ said Mr. Jaggers, placing a hand on my arm and smiling openly, ‘this man must be the cleverest impostor in London.’

‘Not at all,’ Wemmick answered, growing bolder by the moment. ‘I think you’re one yourself.’

They exchanged the same peculiar looks again, each still apparently suspecting the other of deceiving him.

‘You have a pleasant home?’ Mr. Jaggers said.

‘Since it doesn’t interfere with business,’ Wemmick replied, ‘leave it at that. Looking at you now, sir, I wouldn’t be surprised if you were making plans for a pleasant home of your own someday, once you’re tired of all this work.’

Mr. Jaggers nodded two or three times, as though remembering something, and actually sighed. ‘Pip,’ he said, ‘let’s leave “poor dreams” alone. Your experience of them is much more recent, so you know more about them than I do. But about this other matter: I’ll give you a hypothetical case. Remember, I’m admitting nothing.’

He waited until I said I fully understood his explicit statement that he admitted nothing.

‘Now, Pip,’ Mr. Jaggers continued, ‘imagine this situation. Suppose a woman, in the circumstances you have described, kept her child hidden and was compelled to tell her legal adviser about it because he explained that, to determine the scope of her defence, he needed to know the truth about that child.’
